chunks: Concerning the water, he said: “There is nothing wrong with it; stir the water with the bucket.”
Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥasan said: What is meant here is when it has not decomposed, because if it has decomposed, seven buckets are drawn from it, as we explained in the first report.
Then he said, may Allah the Exalted support him: If a sparrow or something similar falls into it, one bucket is drawn from it.
It has already been mentioned earlier in the hadith of ʿAmr ibn Saʿīd al-Madāʾinī, from Muṣaddiq ibn Ṣadaqah, from ʿAmmār al-Sābāṭī, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said:
Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام was asked—and he mentioned the hadith until he said: “And the least of what falls into the well is a sparrow; one bucket is drawn from it.”

Then he said, may Allah the Exalted support him: If droppings of sheep, camels, or gazelles, and their urine, fall into it, it is not rendered impure by that. The same ruling applies to the dung and urine of animals whose meat is eaten: the water is not spoiled by it, and neither the garment nor the body becomes impure by contact with it, except specifically the droppings of scavenger-fed chickens; if that falls into a small quantity of water, five buckets are drawn from it, and if it reaches the garment or body, washing it with water is obligatory.

If it has been established by what we have presented from the verse and the reports that whatever the name of water applies to remains under the ruling of purity, unless something certainly known to be impurity comes upon it, such that one must avoid using it, then these things he mentioned are not among what the Shari'ah prohibits using the water that they have touched or entered. Therefore, the ruling of purity upon it must remain. Likewise, judging a garment impure through contact with such things requires a legal proof, and there is no proof in the Shari'ah that these things render garments impure, so their ruling must remain upon the apparent presumption of purity.
What further confirms that, by way of transmitted report, is what he narrated:

key_terms.اَلشَّرِيعَةِ: the revealed law that determines whether impurity is established
key_terms.اَلطَّهَارَةِ: ritual purity as the default legal state of water and things
key_terms.اَلْبِئْرِ: a well, specifically discussed regarding contaminants falling into it
key_terms.اَلْمَاءِ: water, the central subject of the legal ruling
key_terms.خَمْسُ دِلَاءٍ: five buckets to be drawn out in a specified case
key_terms.دَلْوٌ وَاحِدٌ: one bucket to be drawn out in a specified case
key_terms.ذَرْقَ اَلدَّجَاجِ اَلْجَلَّالَةِ: the droppings of scavenger-fed chickens, treated as an exception in the ruling
key_terms.نَجَاسَةٌ: a legally recognized impurity that changes the ruling of use

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on well water or small amounts of water when birds, animal droppings, or urine fall into it?
ai.summary: This passage discusses legal rulings on the purity of water when certain animals, droppings, or similar substances fall into it. It affirms the principle that water remains upon taharah (ritual purity) unless a definite najasah is established by Shar'i proof, and it cites hadith evidence for specific cases.
